data.name: Canada
data.summary: Canada taxes residents on worldwide income at combined federal and provincial rates; figures here use Ontario (Toronto) as the representative province. Half of a capital gain is taxable, giving a top rate of about 26.8% in Ontario (24.0% Alberta, 26.7% Quebec); the 2024 proposal to raise the inclusion rate to two-thirds is not in force (PwC's 2026 summary still states the 50% inclusion). Eligible Canadian dividends are taxed at up to 39.3% and foreign dividends as ordinary income at up to 53.5%. There is no inheritance, gift or wealth tax, but death (and gifts to children) trigger a deemed disposition at market value, so accrued gains are taxed at about 26.8% at each generation, plus provincial probate fees (Ontario 1.5% of the estate above CAD 50,000). Leaving Canada triggers a departure tax on accrued gains.

regimes.name: Canadian tax resident (Ontario)
regimes.description: Worldwide income taxed at federal + provincial rates; Ontario used as representative province.
regimes.eligibility: Resident from the day significant residential ties (home, spouse, dependants) are established; 183-day deeming rule for sojourners. Non-citizens need permanent or temporary residence status.

capital_gains.summary: 50% of a capital gain is included in income and taxed at ordinary rates. 2026 combined top rates on capital gains: Ontario 26.8%, British Columbia 26.8%, Quebec 26.7%, Alberta 24.0% (top federal bracket from CAD 258,482 at 33%). The proposed increase of the inclusion rate to two-thirds for gains above CAD 250,000 (Budget 2024) is not law: PwC's 2026 summary states half of a capital gain is taxable and its rate table is based on 50%.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Principal residence exemption (one per family unit per year). Lifetime capital gains exemption for qualified small business corporation shares (amount not verified in this session).
capital_gains.regional_differences: Top combined capital gains rates 2026: Ontario 26.8%, BC 26.8%, Quebec 26.7%, Alberta 24.0% (other provinces not checked).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Deemed disposition at fair market value on death (ITA s. 70(5)), on gifts to anyone other than a spouse (s. 69), and on emigration (s. 128.1; departure tax, deferrable with security above CAD 16,500 of federal tax). Assets owned when the person last became resident are excluded from departure tax if resident 60 months or less in the prior 10 years. Arrivals generally get a cost step-up to market value on immigration (s. 128.1(1); not verified from an opened source). Alternative minimum tax was reformed from 2024 (details not verified here).

capital_gains.rate_basis: Ontario 2026 top combined marginal rate 53.5% x 50% inclusion = 26.8% (PwC table). Private business sale before any lifetime capital gains exemption; real estate other than the principal residence. Foreign tax on gains is creditable.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Frequent trading can make gains business income, 100% taxable at up to 53.5% in Ontario. Taxpayers can elect (s. 39(4)) to treat Canadian securities as capital property.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: No holding period; all capital gains are 50% included.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide gains taxed; foreign property costing over CAD 100,000 must be reported (T1135; threshold not verified in this session).

dividends.summary: Eligible dividends from Canadian public companies are grossed up 38% with a federal dividend tax credit of 15.02% (plus provincial credit): top combined rate Ontario 39.3% (Alberta 34.3%, BC 36.5%, Quebec 40.1%). Non-eligible dividends: Ontario 47.7%. Foreign dividends get no gross-up or credit and are taxed as ordinary income (Ontario top 53.5%), with a foreign tax credit capped at 15% of the dividend; excess foreign tax is deductible only.
dividends.regional_differences: Top eligible dividend rates 2026: Ontario 39.3%, BC 36.5%, Alberta 34.3%, Quebec 40.1%; ordinary income (foreign dividends) Ontario/BC 53.5%, Quebec 53.3%, Alberta 48.0%.
dividends.important_exceptions: Foreign non-business tax credit limited to 15% of property income; any withholding above 15% is only deductible. Offshore investment fund property and FAPI rules can attribute passive income of controlled foreign companies.

dividends.rate_basis: Ontario 2026 top combined rates (PwC): eligible dividends 39.3%; foreign dividends are ordinary income at 53.5%, with credit for source WHT up to 15%.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 25% WHT on dividends paid to non-residents, reduced to 5-20% by treaty.
dividends.treaty_network: 94 tax treaties (Russia suspended from 18 November 2024), including the US (15% on portfolio dividends).
dividends.holding_company_notes: Passive investment income of a Canadian-controlled private corporation is taxed at about 50% (federal 38 2/3% including 10 2/3% refundable tax, plus provincial), refundable on payment of dividends; integration largely removes any deferral advantage. No holding structure is modelled because none gives this family a material advantage: interest and foreign dividends bear about 50% in the corporation and gains about 25% (half taxable), with the refundable part returned only when taxable dividends are paid, so after payout the total is close to personal holding; an estate freeze can shift future growth to the children but the deemed disposal at death still applies to the frozen shares (and later to the children's), a family trust holding growth shares has its own 21-year deemed disposal, and the corporate attribution rule (ITA s. 74.4) and TOSI limit income splitting with a spouse or minor children for a pure investment company.

wealth_tax.summary: No net wealth tax at federal or provincial level.

wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Municipal property tax on market value. Provincial land transfer taxes on purchases (generally up to 5%), plus surcharges on foreign buyers: Ontario 25% non-resident speculation tax, Toronto a further 10% municipal tax, BC 20% for foreign entities in specified areas; BC speculation and vacancy tax 3% for foreign owners in 2026. The federal underused housing tax was eliminated from the 2025 calendar year.

inheritance.summary: No inheritance, estate or gift tax federally or in any province. However, a deceased person is deemed to have sold all capital property at market value immediately before death, so accrued gains are taxed in the final return at the capital gains rate (Ontario top 26.8%), except where property passes to a spouse or spousal trust (rollover). Gifts to children likewise trigger a deemed sale at market value. Ontario charges estate administration tax of 1.5% on the value of a probated estate above CAD 50,000.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: No inheritance tax of any amount. Ontario EAT: 0 up to CAD 50,000, then CAD 15 per CAD 1,000 (1.5%). Spousal rollover defers the deemed disposition to the second death.
inheritance.regional_differences: Probate fees vary: Ontario 1.5% above CAD 50,000; other provinces have lower or capped fees (Alberta, Quebec low; not verified in this session).
inheritance.important_exceptions: The deemed disposition at death is in substance a tax on the transfer to children (about 26.8% of the unrealised gain, not of the whole value). It is not captured in the inheritance brackets here; see open questions. Assets held outside the probated will (joint ownership, secondary wills for private shares in Ontario) can reduce EAT.

open_questions: Deemed-disposal rate set to the Ontario top capital gains rate (26.76% = 53.53% x 50% inclusion); the effective charge depends on the unrealised gain in the estate (the scoring model assumes 40% of the estate).
inheritance.spouse_note: No inheritance tax, but death triggers a deemed disposition of capital property (Income Tax Act s. 70(5)). The spousal rollover in s. 70(6) defers it (property passes at cost) only if the deceased and the spouse or common-law partner were resident in Canada and the property vests indefeasibly in the spouse, or a qualifying spousal trust, within 36 months; it is a deferral, taxed when the spouse sells or dies, and the executor may elect out (s. 70(6.2)).
inheritance.gift_tax: No gift tax, but a gift of appreciated property is a deemed disposition at fair market value, taxing the donor's accrued gain (Ontario top 26.8%). Attribution rules can attribute income on gifts to minor children back to the parent.
inheritance.business_relief: Lifetime capital gains exemption on qualified small business corporation shares reduces the deemed-disposition gain; estate freezes are common.
inheritance.foreign_assets: Deemed disposition at death covers worldwide capital property of a Canadian resident.
inheritance.domicile_rules: Residence-based; no domicile concept. Departure tax on emigration (s. 128.1) means no tail of deemed-disposition exposure after leaving, but the gain is taxed on exit.

residency.tax_residency_test: Factual residence based on residential ties (home, spouse/partner and dependants in Canada are significant ties; secondary ties include property, bank accounts, health coverage); deemed resident if present 183 days or more in a year. Newcomers usually become resident on the day they arrive with significant ties.

data.us_citizen_notes: US citizens in Canada file in both countries; Canada credits US tax only on US-source income, and the US credits Canadian tax. Mismatches: Canadian TFSAs/RESPs are not tax-favoured for the US, Canadian mutual funds are PFICs, and Canada's deemed disposition at death can coincide with the US estate tax (treaty Article XXIX-B on taxes at death; not verified here). Treaty relief for this overlap exists but was not verified in this session.
open_questions: The official Department of Finance / Prime Minister notice of the March 2025 cancellation of the inclusion-rate increase could still not be opened: canada.ca returned 404 for the release URLs tried (department-finance/news/2025/03/... and pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2025/03/21/...) and the news search page needs JavaScript; the CRA 'What's new - capital gains' page opened but does not mention the cancellation. The 50% rate rests on PwC's 2026 summary.

The schema has no field for a deemed capital gains disposition at death; inheritance is coded as basis 'none' with the deemed disposition explained in text. A scoring model should treat death as a realisation event at the capital gains rate.

income.name: Canada

income_tax.summary: Canadian residents pay federal tax (14% to 33% in 2026) plus Ontario tax (5.05% to 13.16%) and Ontario surtaxes of 20% and 36% on provincial tax; the combined top marginal rate in Ontario is 53.53% above CAD 258,482. Employees pay CPP (5.95% to CAD 74,600 plus CPP2 above it) and EI; the self-employed pay both CPP shares and may opt out of EI.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Self-employed pay both CPP shares: 11.9% on pensionable earnings between CAD 3,500 and CAD 74,600 (CRA: maximum CAD 8,460.90 for 2026) plus CPP2 (both shares) on earnings from CAD 74,600 to about CAD 85,000; PwC's maximum for self-employed is CAD 9,292.90 (CPP2 part CAD 832, derived; the CPP2 rate and second ceiling were not on an opened page). The rate recorded, 0.10933, is that maximum spread over the CAD 85,000 cap, an approximation of the basic exemption and CPP2 steps. Half of base CPP and all CPP2 are deductible. Self-employed people are not liable for EI premiums unless they opt in (EI 2026: 1.63% to CAD 68,900, maximum CAD 1,123.07, CRA). Deductibility for the self-employed differs: they deduct the employer-equivalent half of the base CPP (3,519.45), both shares of the enhanced CPP (1,422.00) and both shares of CPP2 (832.00), i.e. 5,773.45 of the 9,292.90 maximum, about 0.62, against 0.195 for an employee; the employee figure governs the field. The other half of the base CPP and EI give a federal 15% credit that is not modelled.
income_tax.local_tax_note: Toronto has no municipal income tax; combined figures are federal + Ontario with the 20%/36% surtax built in. Combined marginal rates are computed from the opened federal and Ontario tables before non-refundable credits: surtax thresholds (provincial tax of CAD 5,818 and 7,446) are reached at about CAD 87,729 and 105,521 of taxable income. The Ontario Health Premium (up to CAD 900) is not included and the credit amounts that shift the surtax thresholds slightly are ignored.

open_questions: Combined brackets re-derived on 2026-10-15 from the PwC federal table (14/20.5/26/29/33% at 58,523/117,045/181,440/258,482) and the EY Ontario table and surtax thresholds (CAD 5,818 and 7,446): every listed combined rate reproduces (e.g. 19.05%, 29.65%, 31.48%, 34.77%, 37.91%, 43.41%, 53.53%). The CRA and Ontario pages themselves were not read.

Non-refundable credits are not modelled: the federal basic personal amount (EY: CAD 14,829 plus up to CAD 1,623 additional, i.e. up to CAD 16,452, worth about CAD 2,300 at 14%) and Ontario credits reduce tax; the Ontario surtax thresholds are applied to tax before credits, so the 31.48% and 34.77% brackets in reality start at somewhat higher incomes. Ontario low-income tax reduction (no provincial tax up to CAD 18,930) and Ontario Health Premium also ignored. Net effect: tax is overstated by roughly CAD 2,500-3,000 at the persona incomes.

Employee rate 0.0773 is derived: PwC's maximum employee CPP (CAD 4,646.45 including CPP2) plus maximum EI (CAD 1,123.07; CRA confirms 1.63% to CAD 68,900) = CAD 5,769.52, divided by the CAD 74,600 maximum pensionable earnings. CRA confirms base CPP 5.95%, maximum CAD 4,230.45 (employee) and CAD 8,460.90 (self-employed) for 2026.
CPP2 maximum (CAD 416 employee, CAD 832 self-employed) is inferred as the difference between PwC's and CRA's maximums; the CPP2 rate and ceiling page returned 404.

Canada gives credits rather than deductions for base CPP (4.95%, line 30800) and EI. social_security_deductible = 0.195 is the approximate deductible share only (enhanced CPP + CPP2 over CPP + CPP2 + EI); the 2026 base/enhanced split (4.95%/1.00%) is the CRA 2025 line 30800/22215 maximums (3,356.10 and 678.00 on 67,800) carried forward, and CPP2 (4% to 85,000) was not read on an opened CRA page. The credit value is not modelled.

income.residence_routes: There is no digital nomad visa; visitors may not work for Canadian clients and generally may work remotely for foreign employers only as short-stay visitors. Skilled employees enter through Express Entry (permanent residence) or an employer-specific work permit (LMIA or exempt, such as intra-company transfers and CUSMA professionals for US and Mexican citizens); EU nationals may qualify for International Experience Canada working-holiday permits in some countries. Canada taxes residents on worldwide income and its resident definition rests on residential ties rather than a day count.

succession.name: Canada
succession.summary: Succession law is provincial. In the common-law provinces and in Quebec a person may leave an estate freely, but courts can order support for a spouse and dependants (e.g. Ontario Succession Law Reform Act Part V) and a surviving spouse has family-property claims. Trusts are widely used and the Hague Trusts Convention is in force for most provinces, not Quebec. Private foundations exist only as charities.
succession.family_claims: Common-law provinces: courts may order support or a share for a spouse, children and dependants (e.g. Ontario SLRA Part V s. 58; British Columbia Wills, Estates and Succession Act s. 60; Alberta Wills and Succession Act Part 5), and a spouse may elect an equalisation under family law (e.g. Ontario Family Law Act s. 6). Quebec: freedom of testation, but spouse partition of the family patrimony on death and alimentary claims within 6 months (Civil Code arts. 684 ff.). Specific articles were not read here and are from general knowledge.
succession.foreign_law_note: Not sourced. The general conflict rule is the domicile for movables and the location for land; whether a testator may designate foreign law (Civil Code of Québec arts. 3098 ff.) was not verified.
succession.trust_note: HCCH table: Canada ratified 20 Oct 1992, in force 1 Jan 1993, with declarations and reservations, and extension noted by footnote 9, so it applies only to the provinces that implemented it (Nova Scotia's International Trusts Act is one). Quebec and any other non-extended unit are outside it. Provinces have trust law (Quebec: Civil Code arts. 1260-1298). Foundations: Quebec Civil Code arts. 1256-1259 allow foundations for general-interest purposes; elsewhere private foundations are registered charities (Income Tax Act s. 149.1). Canada taxes trusts, including a 21-year deemed disposition (ITA s. 104(4)); not read here.
open_questions: The HCCH footnote 9 listing which provinces and territories the Convention extends to was not retrievable from the page; confirm.
Quebec's rule on choosing the law applicable to a succession (Civil Code arts. 3098 ff.) was not read.
Provincial family-provision statutes and article numbers were cited from general knowledge; verify each.
Ontario and other provincial trust-registration or tax rules (T3 reporting, bare trust rules) not covered.

immigration.name: Canada
immigration.summary: No one can buy Canadian residence at federal level in 2026: the federal investor programme ended in 2014 and the Start-up Visa has taken no new applications since 31 December 2025. Quebec's investor programme (CAD 1.2 million, mostly refundable) is the only passive route. Everyone else uses points-based Express Entry or a provincial nomination. EU, US and other passports are treated alike.
immigration.naturalisation: Permanent residents need 1,095 days (3 years) in Canada in the 5 years before applying (730 days as a PR), tax filing for 3 of 5 years, language CLB 4 and a knowledge test for ages 18 to 54.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: Canada allows dual citizenship, but the applicant's other country may not.

routes.name: Start-up Visa (permanent residence)
routes.status_note: Paused to new applications from 31 December 2025; grace for 2025 commitment-certificate holders ended 30 June 2026; replacement pilot announced without details.
routes.summary: Permanent residence for founders backed by a designated Canadian investor group, incubator or accelerator. Paused: new applications stopped on 31 December 2025.
routes.requirements: A commitment certificate from a designated organisation, a qualifying business, language CLB 5 and settlement funds. IRCC stopped accepting new permanent residence applications at 11:59 pm on 31 December 2025 (Start-up Visa work permits ended 19 December 2025); applicants with a valid 2025 commitment certificate could apply until 30 June 2026. IRCC's 2026-27 departmental plan mentions a new 'high impact' start-up visa pilot with no dates announced.
routes.physical_presence: PR holders must be in Canada 730 days in any 5 years to keep status
routes.tax_note: Becoming a Canadian resident makes worldwide income taxable in Canada.

routes.summary: Canada's passive-investor immigration programmes are closed: the federal Immigrant Investor Program ended in 2014 and its venture-capital replacement is no longer open.
routes.requirements: The Immigrant Investor Program (a CAD 800,000 five-year interest-free loan to a province) was terminated in February 2014. The 2015 Immigrant Investor Venture Capital pilot (net worth CAD 10 million, CAD 2 million non-guaranteed investment over 15 years, 60 visas) is no longer open. No federal passive-investor route exists in 2026.

routes.name: Quebec Immigrant Investor Program (QIIP)
routes.summary: Quebec selects investors who place CAD 1,000,000 with a government-listed intermediary for 5 years (returned without interest) and donate CAD 200,000. Federal permanent residence follows. Relaunched 1 January 2024 with intake caps.
routes.requirements: Net worth at least CAD 2,000,000; CAD 1,200,000 total (CAD 1,000,000 refundable after 5 years, CAD 200,000 non-refundable); 2 years of management experience in the last 5; oral French at level 7 (B2); secondary diploma; age 18+. Intake cap 1,900 applications per period (1,330 China/Hong Kong/Macao, 570 others); periods are announced when open. All figures from one law-firm guide dated June 2026, not the MIFI page.
routes.investment_options: CAD 1,000,000 is refundable after 5 years; the net cost is the CAD 200,000 donation plus lost returns.
routes.fees_note: MIFI application fee per SiLaw; federal PR fees not included.
routes.physical_presence: Intent to settle in Quebec; PR holders need 730 days in any 5 years
routes.processing_time: About 2.5 to 3.5 years in total per SiLaw (12 to 18 months MIFI, 18 to 24 months IRCC)
routes.family: Spouse and dependent children included in the application.
routes.tax_note: Quebec residents pay Canadian federal and Quebec income tax on worldwide income.

routes.name: Express Entry skilled worker programmes
routes.summary: Points-based permanent residence for skilled workers (Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Worker, Federal Skilled Trades), with a provincial nominee option. No investment is needed.
routes.requirements: Language CLB 7 (CLB 5 for some trades and TEER 2/3 jobs); one year of skilled work experience (in Canada for the Canadian Experience Class); secondary education for Federal Skilled Worker; a job offer only for Skilled Trades. Candidates are ranked and invited. US citizens have no special access beyond temporary CUSMA work categories (not researched).
